issues.legal_issue: The government may exempt an entire scheduled industry, including large undertakings, from licensing where the industry’s stage of development supports the exemption, and the authority to do so is not an excessive delegation of legislative power.
material_facts: The sugar industry was a scheduled industry subject to compulsory licensing.
The government removed sugar from the industries requiring compulsory licensing, relying on the development of the industry and the recommendations of committees.
The challenge argued that an exemption could not cover large industries and that the exemption power was excessive delegation.
issues.conclusion: The exemption power covered an industry-wide exemption, including large industries, and the delegation was not excessive.
issues.legal_principle: Section 29B(1) of the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951 permits exemption of a scheduled industry or class of industries from some or all requirements of the Act, having regard to specified factors that include the stage of development of the industry. The statutory policy and grounds for exemption provide adequate guidance, so the power is not excessive delegation. The Court relied on P.J. Irani v. State of Madras, Sitaram Bishambar Dayal v. State of U.P., Mahe Beach Trading Co. v. Union Territory of Pondicherry, State of Tamil Nadu v. K. Sabhanayagam, Consumer Action Group v. State of Tamil Nadu, and Kishan Prakash Sharma v. Union of India.

predicates.industry_wide_exemption_challenged: A party challenged an exemption that removed a whole scheduled industry from a licensing requirement.
predicates.government_relied_on_industry_developmen: The government relied on the industry’s stage of development in deciding to grant the exemption.
predicates.exemption_power_covers_industry_stage: The governing exemption power permits exemptions based on an industry’s stage of development.

issues.definition: When an industry-wide exemption is challenged, the government relied on the industry’s development, and the exemption power covers that ground, the exemption is authorized.

issues.legal_issue: The executive may remove an industry’s licensing requirement by a notification made under an existing statutory exemption power, without amending the statute or obtaining parliamentary approval for the notification.
material_facts: The government issued a notification under its statutory exemption power that removed sugar from the list of industries requiring compulsory licensing.
The challenge argued that de-licensing required legislative action and questioned the absence of parliamentary approval for the notification.
issues.conclusion: The notification was sufficient to de-license the industry; the statute did not require amendment or parliamentary approval of the notification.
issues.legal_principle: Article 73(1) of the Constitution makes the Union’s executive power co-extensive with its legislative power, and the existing statutory exemption power authorized the notification. The Act contained no requirement that such a notification be approved by Parliament. The Court also relied on P.T.R. Exports (Madras) Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India for the principle that the power to frame policy includes the power to withdraw or change it.

predicates.executive_policy_notification_challenged: A party challenged an executive notification changing an industry’s licensing requirements.
predicates.notification_issued_under_exemption_auth: The executive issued the notification under an existing statutory power to grant exemptions.

issues.definition: When a challenged notification changing licensing requirements was issued under an existing exemption power, the executive may remove the licensing requirement by notification.

issues.legal_issue: Courts should not invalidate economic policy choices unless they clearly violate law or the Constitution or are shockingly arbitrary.
material_facts: The government adopted de-licensing as part of its economic policy after committee recommendations and consideration of the industry’s development.
The challengers disputed the policy and the process by which it was adopted, but no violation of law was shown in the notification or press note.
The lower court had relied on suspicions and conjectures about illegality and unfairness.
issues.conclusion: The economic policy was not open to invalidation on the grounds advanced, and the notification and press note were valid.
issues.legal_principle: Courts ordinarily defer to executive and legislative choices in economic and fiscal matters, and do not assess their relative wisdom. Judicial intervention is limited to clear statutory or constitutional violation, or arbitrariness so extreme as to be shockingly arbitrary. The Court relied on Balco Employees’ Union v. Union of India, Premium Granites v. State of Tamil Nadu, M.P. Oil Extraction v. State of M.P., Ugar Sugar Works Ltd. v. Delhi Administration, Bhavesh D. Parish v. Union of India, Netai Bag v. State of West Bengal, Prag Ice & Oil Mills v. Union of India, Sitaram Sugar Co. Ltd. v. Union of India, India Cement Ltd. v. Union of India, and Divisional Manager, Aravali Golf Club v. Chander Hass. It also stated that legitimate expectation does not restrict an authority’s choice where it is empowered to decide policy.

predicates.economic_policy_challenge: A party asked a court to invalidate a government choice concerning economic or regulatory policy.
predicates.no_clear_legal_or_constitutional_conflic: The record did not show a clear conflict between the policy and a legal or constitutional requirement.
predicates.policy_not_shockingly_arbitrary: The policy was not shown to be shockingly arbitrary.

issues.definition: When an economic policy is challenged but no clear legal or constitutional conflict or shocking arbitrariness is shown, the policy is not invalidated.

issues.legal_issue: A distance safeguard for new sugar mills applies retrospectively to pending disputes when the governing amendment is clarificatory and retrospective.
material_facts: The challenge to de-licensing rested on the establishment of a sugar mill in the vicinity of an existing mill, though more than the prescribed minimum distance away.
A later amendment specified effective steps for establishing a mill.
A prior Supreme Court decision held that the amendment was clarificatory and retrospective and upheld the minimum-distance requirement.
issues.conclusion: The distance safeguard applied retrospectively to pending disputes, substantially removing the basis of the challenge to de-licensing.
issues.legal_principle: In Ojas Industries P. Ltd. v. Oudh Sugar Mills Ltd., the Court held that the amendments to the Sugarcane (Control) Order, 1966, specifying effective steps, were clarificatory and retrospective and applied to cases pending before courts; it also upheld the minimum-distance requirement between mills.

predicates.pending_mill_spacing_dispute: A dispute concerning the spacing of a newly established mill was pending before a court.
predicates.clarificatory_amendment_specifies_effect: A later amendment clarified the steps required to establish a mill.
predicates.amendment_applies_retroactively: The amendment was held to apply retrospectively to pending disputes.

issues.definition: When a mill-spacing dispute is pending and a clarificatory amendment specifying establishment steps applies retrospectively, the spacing safeguard applies to that dispute.
